section.title: The Oracle against the Philistines
section.sectionRationale: The second panel in the oracles against the nations turns from Egypt to Philistia, Judah's coastal neighbor and ancient enemy. A flood from the north sweeps away Gaza, Ashkelon, and the remnant of Caphtor, and the chapter ends by asking the one question that matters: how long until the sword of the LORD can rest, and the answer is, not until His purpose is finished.
section.thesis: The sword of the LORD moves against the Philistines because He has appointed it, and it cannot rest until His commanded work is done.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the word against the Philistines before Gaza's fall; the flood rising from the north; the day appointed to destroy the Philistines; and the sword of the LORD, unable to rest until it finishes its errand.

units.label: The word against the Philistines before Gaza's fall

verses.text: This is the word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah the prophet about the Philistines before Pharaoh struck down Gaza.

units.label: The flood rising from the north

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “See how the waters are rising from the north and becoming an overflowing torrent. They will overflow the land and its fullness, the cities and their inhabitants. The people will cry out, and all who dwell in the land will wail
at the sound of the galloping hooves of stallions, the rumbling of chariots, and the clatter of their wheels. The fathers will not turn back for their sons; their hands will hang limp.

units.label: The day appointed to destroy the Philistines

verses.text: For the day has come to destroy all the Philistines, to cut off from Tyre and Sidon every remaining ally. Indeed, the LORD is about to destroy the Philistines, the remnant from the coasts of Caphtor.
The people of Gaza will shave their heads in mourning; Ashkelon will be silenced. O remnant of their valley, how long will you gash yourself?

units.label: The sword of the LORD cannot rest

verses.text: ‘Alas, O {{chereb|sword}} of the LORD, how long until you rest? Return to your {{taar|sheath}}; cease and be still!’
How can it rest when the LORD has commanded it? He has appointed it against Ashkelon and the shore of its coastland.”

chereb.gloss: Sword. Here personified and even addressed directly, 'O sword of the LORD', as though it were a living agent of divine justice that cannot simply be told to stop.

taar.gloss: Sheath or scabbard, the same word used elsewhere for a razor or blade case. The plea to return the sword to its sheath pictures a desperate wish for judgment to cease, answered immediately by the reminder that the LORD Himself has commanded and appointed it.

basic.context: This short oracle turns from Egypt to Philistia, the coastal enemy that had harassed Israel since the days of the judges and the era of Samson, Saul, and David. Dated loosely to an Egyptian campaign against Gaza, it pictures an invading flood from the north sweeping the land, silencing the great Philistine cities of Gaza and Ashkelon, and ends with an almost pleading question: how long until the sword can rest, answered by the sober truth that it cannot, because the LORD Himself has sent it.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical oracle against a real ancient people, substantially fulfilled in Babylon's westward campaigns that devastated the Philistine coastal cities in the early sixth century BC. It is not a timeless verdict on any modern nation bearing a similar name; the enduring truth is that the LORD directs even the most terrifying invasions toward His own appointed purposes, and no one, not even the sword itself, can call a halt before He is finished.
basic.originalLanguages: The chereb, sword, of verse 6 is addressed directly, as though pleading with it to return to its ta'ar, its sheath, and rest. The poignant personification only deepens the point of verse 7: the sword cannot obey that plea, because it obeys a higher command, the LORD who appointed it against Ashkelon and her coastland.
basic.typology: The sword commanded and unable to rest until its errand is finished anticipates the certainty of final judgment in Christ's hands, an assignment that likewise cannot be recalled or turned aside once given, Revelation 19:15.
basic.christ: The sword of the LORD cannot rest until it has done what it was sent to do, verse 7, a picture of divine justice too resolute to be talked down. That same certainty belongs to Christ, who alone will execute the last judgment precisely as appointed, neither early nor late, and who alone, unlike this sword, can also sheath wrath forever for those who take refuge in Him, having already borne its edge at the cross.
basic.god: God is sovereign even over the timing of judgment: an invading flood, a sword unable to rest, all move exactly on His schedule and toward His purpose, not by chance and not beyond His command. His government of history reaches every coastline, not only Israel's own land.
basic.crossReferences: Amos 1:6-8 pronounces a related judgment on the Philistine cities. Zephaniah 2:4-7 promises the coastland will one day belong to the remnant of Judah. Ezekiel 25:15-17 gives a parallel oracle against Philistia. Revelation 19:15 pictures Christ's own sword of final judgment.
basic.oneStory: This brief oracle shows a sword that cannot rest until the LORD's appointed work is finished, a certainty of judgment that runs all the way to Christ, who alone executes the last judgment exactly as commanded, and who alone can turn that same sword's wrath aside for all who are found in Him.

context.literary:
Jeremiah 47 is the shortest of the oracles against the nations in chapters 46 to 51, and it is built like a single wave. A one verse superscription, verse 1, sets the occasion. Then the poetry moves in four beats: water rising, verses 2 and 3; a day fixed and a coast stripped of its allies, verses 4 and 5; a cry to the sword, verse 6; and a flat answer, verse 7. The poem is held together by one idea, that a force which looks like politics is really an appointment. The flood comes from the north, the sword has been commanded, and the last line says that the LORD has appointed it against a named city and a named shore.

The imagery escalates by scale and then by sound. The flood overflows the land and everything in it, the cities and their inhabitants, verse 2. Then the poet lets the hearer listen to what the flood is made of: galloping hooves, the rumbling of chariots, the clatter of wheels, verse 3. The most striking human detail follows. Fathers do not turn back for their sons, and their hands hang limp. Panic has cancelled the oldest instinct there is, and the hands that should reach for a child have gone slack.

The speakers shift in a way that is easy to miss. The LORD speaks in verses 2 to 4. In verse 5 the poem turns to address the survivors directly, a question put to the remnant of their valley. Verse 6 is a cry in the first person, 'Alas, O sword of the LORD', and verse 7 answers it by asking its own rhetorical question. The poem ends in a refusal, not a consolation, which is unusual in the oracles against the nations and fits the grim brevity of the whole chapter. Unlike Moab, Ammon and Elam in chapters 48 and 49, no promise of restoration closes this oracle.
context.historical:
The Philistines were not a native people of Canaan. Amos 9:7 says the LORD brought them up 'from Caphtor,' and Deuteronomy 2:23 remembers the Caphtorites settling as far as Gaza. The BSB footnote at Jeremiah 47:4 gives Caphtor as Crete, and the oracle calls them 'the remnant from the coasts of Caphtor,' a deliberate reminder that they were newcomers from across the sea. They settled a chain of city states on the southern coast: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath. From the judges to David they were Israel's most persistent military rival, as Goliath of Gath, 1 Samuel 17:4, and the ark story of 1 Samuel 4 to 6 recall. Uzziah later broke into their walls, 2 Chronicles 26:6, but they outlived the Israelite kingdoms of the north.

The oracle is dated by an event in verse 1, 'before Pharaoh struck down Gaza.' Egypt contested the coast through the last decades of the seventh century BC. Most readers link the blow to an Egyptian campaign under Pharaoh Neco, whose army meets its defeat at Carchemish, Jeremiah 46:2. The text does not say which Pharaoh, so the exact year is not certain, and the point is that the word was spoken beforehand. Verse 4 also lists Tyre and Sidon as the Philistines' remaining allies, and Ezekiel 26:2-3 and Isaiah 23:1 show that Tyre was marked for judgment too.

The flood is not Egypt. The north in Jeremiah is the standing direction of Babylon, and Jeremiah 25:9 already names Nebuchadnezzar as the servant the LORD will bring against the surrounding nations. Babylonian records, which are outside Scripture, report the sack of Ashkelon in 604 BC, and a coastal power that had traded with Egypt and the sea for centuries was then taken apart. First hearers in Jerusalem, in a Judah lying on the same invasion road, would have understood that the water was rising toward them as well.
context.canonical:
Philistia is one of the best attested objects of prophetic judgment. Amos 1:6-8 charges Gaza with exiling a whole population, and the same verse names Ashkelon's ruler as one to be cut off. Zephaniah 2:4-7 plays on the city names, 'Gaza will be abandoned,' and then turns to pasture: the coast will belong to the remnant of the house of Judah. Ezekiel 25:15-17 gives the motive as 'ancient hostility' and 'vengeance with malice of soul.' Isaiah 14:29-31 warns the Philistines not to rejoice that the rod that struck them is broken, because a cloud of smoke is coming from the north. Jeremiah 47 therefore stands in a long chorus, and it adds the sword that will not sheathe.

The water image has its own history. Isaiah 8:7-8 describes the king of Assyria as the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates that overflow Judah, 'reaching up to the neck.' Psalm 124:4-5 gives the people's side of the same picture, floods that would have swept them away if the LORD had not been on their side. Jeremiah borrows a metaphor his hearers already knew and aims it outward.

The sword that will not rest is Jeremiah's recurring word for judgment. 'The sword of the LORD devours from one end of the earth to the other,' Jeremiah 12:12. Ezekiel 21:3-5 pictures the LORD drawing His sword from its sheath 'not to return it again,' and Ezekiel 21:30 gives the opposite command with the same verb, 'Return the sword to its sheath.' The New Testament carries the sword forward in two directions. Zechariah 13:7 calls the sword against the Shepherd, and Matthew 26:52 shows Jesus telling Peter to put his own sword away. Finally Revelation 19:15 and 19:21 put the sword in the mouth of the returning Christ. And Acts 8:26 sends Philip down 'the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza,' where the gospel reaches an Ethiopian official on the old Philistine road.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah was a man who spent years announcing that Babylon was God's instrument against Judah, and he was hated for it. This chapter does a second job for the same message. It shows that the same hand that threatens Jerusalem also governs the coast. If the flood from the north is a sign of the LORD's government and not merely a stronger army, then Judah cannot console herself that Egypt, or Gaza, or Tyre will somehow stop it. The oracle takes away the neighbours Judah might have counted on as buffers or allies.

The passage also teaches Judah how to hear a sword. Verse 6 is not a calm sentence. It is the sound of someone who cannot stand the sight of the slaughter and begs the sword to stop. The prophet lets that cry stand, and then answers it. That is pastoral honesty. The text does not pretend judgment is painless, and it does not let the pain become a reason to doubt that judgment is real. First hearers were meant to leave sober, with their own city in mind, and with one fixed fact: nobody on the coast has authority to say 'enough.'
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes an event. It does not tell anyone to attack, resent or wish ill on a people. The nearest thing to an imperative in the poem is the cry of verse 6, and that is a plea for peace, not a command for violence. Readers should also notice that the human agents are not named in the poem. The LORD owns the sword, and it is He who 'has appointed it.' That is not a licence for any nation, army or believer to claim the same commission. Scripture reserves that kind of authority to God's own explicit word.

What applies today is a conviction, not a policy: God is the judge of all peoples, and no coastline, no alliance and no trade partner sits outside His reach. The right response is humility about our own security and compassion for those under the sword, never triumph. Jesus teaches the same posture when He weeps over a city, Luke 19:41-44, instead of cheering for its fall.

debates.question: Who is the 'sword of the LORD' in verses 6 and 7, and who is its human edge?

views.label: Babylon, as the instrument of the LORD
views.case: The flood comes from the north, verse 2, and Jeremiah elsewhere names Nebuchadnezzar as the servant the LORD will bring against the surrounding nations, Jeremiah 25:9 and 27:6. Babylon swept the Philistine coast within a generation of this oracle, and the sack of Ashkelon in 604 BC is recorded outside the Bible. On this reading the sword is the Babylonian army, truly the LORD's, truly human.

views.label: Egypt in the first instance, then Babylon
views.case: The superscription places the word 'before Pharaoh struck down Gaza,' verse 1, so some read the first strike as Egyptian. They propose that the oracle's wave language covers two successive attackers, Egypt who hits Gaza first and Babylon who finishes the work, with the 'north' speaking of the final one.

views.label: The judgment itself, personified as God's own weapon
views.case: Others stress that the text never names an army. It speaks of the sword of the LORD and of a flood, and they take both as images of divine judgment in itself, standing for any human instruments, as in Jeremiah 12:12.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the human forces are not the real cause. The sentence of verse 7, 'the LORD has commanded it,' stays fixed whichever army is meant. The historical identification matters less than the theological one, and it should be held with some humility because the passage chooses not to name names.

debates.question: Is the cry of verse 6 the prophet's, the people's, or the sword's own?

views.label: The prophet's lament
views.case: Jeremiah weeps over what he must announce, Jeremiah 8:21 to 9:1, and the heartbreak of verse 6 fits his voice. He then answers his own plea on the LORD's behalf in verse 7.

views.label: The voice of the suffering Philistines
views.case: The question 'how long?' is a standard cry of a people under attack, and the poem can borrow it to show their desperation. The prophet then answers with the refusal that they will not like.

debates.bearing: Either way, the text keeps both truths on the page together, the real horror of what happens and the real authority behind it. It does not allow us to flatten the moment into either heartless fate or senseless disaster.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's central image is the sword, chereb, and its sheath, ta'ar, which the basic level has already named. Three other phrases carry much of the weight, and each is easier to see in the Hebrew.

First, the flood in verse 2 is an overflowing torrent. The verb behind 'overflow,' shataph, is the word Isaiah 8:8 uses of the Assyrian flood that 'will overflow its channels' and sweep into Judah. In both prophets it describes a river that has left its bed, which in the ancient Near East was a picture of an invading army, not a rainstorm. The wadis of the south are dry for most of the year and then fill in an hour, which is exactly how a military collapse feels to those caught in it.

Second, the call to the remnant, 'how long will you gash yourself?' in verse 5, uses the verb gadad, to cut oneself. It is the same root as the prohibition in Deuteronomy 14:1, 'do not cut yourselves or shave your foreheads on behalf of the dead.' The Philistines are mourning in the manner of the surrounding peoples, shaving the head and slashing the flesh, and Israel's law forbade those rites to the sons of the LORD. The detail shows Jeremiah recording their grief in its own customary form, not mocking it. The BSB renders the place name 'their valley' for a word that the footnote reads as 'the Mediterranean coast or plain,' so the phrase points to the whole coastal plain as the place of mourning.

Third, verse 4 gives the Philistines' origin as 'the remnant from the coasts of Caphtor.' The BSB footnote identifies Caphtor as Crete. The Hebrew word for 'coasts' can also be rendered as islands or coastlands, and the whole expression means the sea fringe from which they came. Calling them a remnant is pointed, because 'remnant' is the vocabulary the prophets use of a people that survives by grace. Here it means a people reduced to survivors.

Finally, the verb 'appointed' at the end of verse 7 is the language of a commission. The LORD does not allow the sword to follow its own appetite. He fixes the target, Ashkelon and the shore of its coastland, in the same breath as He fixes the rest. The verse leaves the sword in the position of a servant who has no authority to sheathe itself, which is why the plea of verse 6 can only go unanswered.

typology.type: The sword that cannot sheathe itself, Jeremiah 47:6-7
typology.fulfillment: The sword has been commissioned and must finish its work. In Revelation 19:15 and 19:21 the same weapon appears in the mouth of the returning Christ: 'a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations,' and the rest are killed 'with the sword that proceeded from the mouth of the One seated on the horse.' The escalation is that the sword is no longer carried by a foreign army but is the word of the Rider Himself, Hebrews 4:12. The type falls short because Jeremiah's sword strikes a coast in one century, while Christ's sword judges every nation and ends at the last day.

typology.type: The sword roused against the Shepherd, Zechariah 13:7
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah's poem asks the sword to rest. Zechariah later hears the opposite command, 'Awake, O sword, against My Shepherd,' and Jesus applies that verse to Himself on the night He is arrested, Mark 14:27. When Peter draws a sword, Jesus says 'Put your sword back in its place,' Matthew 26:52, and chooses the cup, John 18:11. The sword that could not rest finally rests on Him. The type is partial because the Philistines' sword fell on the guilty and the sheep, and Christ takes the blow for the sheep.

typology.type: The remnant of the coast and the road to Gaza
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah 9:5-7 promises that after Gaza is cut down, the remnant of the Philistines 'will become like a clan in Judah.' The line of the gospel reaches the old Philistine road at Acts 8:26, where Philip is told to go 'to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.' The type works as a pattern of a judged people who are named inside the promise of a remnant. It falls short in that Acts does not say Philistines are reached, only that the gospel travels the road that bears Gaza's name.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ most directly by the sword. Jeremiah's poem is about a weapon that will not return to its sheath because the LORD has not yet finished with its errand. The Bible's last picture of Jesus is of a Rider whose sword proceeds from His mouth, Revelation 19:15, and it would be a misreading to turn that into a story about Christ's cruelty. The sword in Jeremiah is a fixed verdict, and the Rider is Faithful and True, 'with righteousness He judges and wages war,' Revelation 19:11. What Jeremiah 47 teaches us to expect from Christ is that He will not be talked out of justice by anyone's suffering, including His own people's pain at the sight.

The chapter leads to Christ by the reversal of the poem's one question. The cry of verse 6 asks how long until the sword rests, and verse 7 says it cannot. Zechariah 13:7 then hears the LORD call the sword to wake against the Shepherd. When Jesus is arrested He applies that verse to Himself, Mark 14:27, tells Peter to put away his own sword, Matthew 26:52, and says 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' John 18:11. The place where the sword finally rests is the cross, and it rests there by being turned onto the one Person who could bear it. That is the gospel's answer to the question the poem leaves open.

It leads to Christ by the nations. Zechariah 9:5-7 promises a Philistine remnant that will belong to God. Isaiah 14:29-31 keeps the same coast under sentence. Acts 8:26-39 puts an apostle on the Gaza road, and Acts 2:9-11 hears many nations declare God's wonders, so the line of judgment and mercy over the nations runs through one Person, the Son who has authority both to judge and to include.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Jeremiah 47 itself does not mention a Messiah, a Shepherd or a sacrifice, and the Philistines are not types of Christ's people or His enemies in a coded sense. The link to Christ rests on the New Testament's own use of the sword and the Gentile mission. What this chapter supplies is the problem, a verdict that must be carried out, and the question that Christ answers at His cross: who will stand in the place of the sword, and how can an appointed judgment be satisfied without the guilty being ended?
study.god:
The first thing this chapter says about God is that He governs the movements of armies. The flood is rising, the chariots are rumbling, and yet the text uses the voice of the LORD, 'This is what the LORD says,' to introduce the whole poem. The invading power is never named, and that silence is a theological statement. Whatever the generals thought they were doing, they were not the authors of the event. The same line returns in Isaiah 10:15, where an axe that raises itself above the one who swings it is mocked as absurd.

Second, He is the God of the whole earth and not merely of one nation. The Philistines were never part of the covenant, and the prophet does not appear to offer them a covenant. Yet He addresses them with the same language of 'day' and 'appointment' that He uses of Judah. Amos 9:7 goes further and says He brought the Philistines up from Caphtor as surely as He brought Israel out of Egypt. The God who judges them is the God who gave them their place in history.

Third, God's justice is not impulsive. The sword is appointed against a named city, and the day is fixed, verse 4. That is not a picture of rage lashing out. It is the picture of a commission carried out on a schedule. At the same time the text tolerates the cry of verse 6 as a human response. God is not offended by the sound of someone begging for peace, and the poem makes no attempt to silence it.

Fourth, the passage tells us how God treats pride and hostility without needing to quote them. Ezekiel 25:15 explains Philistia's fate as 'ancient hostility,' and Amos 1:6 as the exile of a whole population. The judgment is not random; it is a response to violence toward His people. Yet the chapter does not make Israel the cause of Philistia's fall. The LORD's own name and purposes are at stake.

For worship, this chapter teaches a certain kind of fear. It is not terror of an unpredictable power, but the settled awe of knowing that history has an owner. It protects believers from thinking that the news cycle has the last word. It also protects us from enjoying judgment. The poem's sword speaks with a voice that sounds like a person at a graveside, and the right posture for a reader is to stay at that graveside. We learn to pray for the nations in the knowledge that the God who judges them has also promised, in Zechariah 9:7, that a remnant from among them will be His.

crossReferences.note: Amos pronounces a parallel judgment on Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron, charging Gaza with exiling a whole population. Read beside Jeremiah, it shows that the same coast had been under sentence for generations, and that the charge was cruelty to others, not simply being Israel's enemy.

Zephaniah plays on the sound of the city names, 'Gaza will be abandoned,' and then promises that the seacoast will become pasture belonging to the remnant of Judah. This is the other half of Jeremiah's grim picture: the place that is emptied becomes a place where the LORD's people find grass.

Ezekiel gives the reason for Philistia's fall as 'ancient hostility' and malice of soul toward Judah, and ends with the statement that they will know that the LORD is the One acting. Jeremiah leaves the reason unstated, and Ezekiel fills it in.

Isaiah warns the Philistines not to rejoice at the fall of the rod that struck them, because a cloud of smoke is coming from the north and there are no stragglers in its ranks. The northern direction and the lack of stragglers anticipate Jeremiah's flood from the north.

After judgment on Ashkelon and Gaza, Zechariah promises that the Philistine remnant will become a remnant for our God, 'like a clan in Judah.' It is the one place that holds out an after-word for the people Jeremiah 47 leaves under sentence.

Here the king of Assyria is the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates that overflow Judah. Jeremiah uses the same flood but sends it against Philistia, showing that the LORD's rising water is not reserved for any one nation.

The LORD says He will draw His sword from its sheath and that 'all flesh will know' it was He, 'not to return it again.' The unsheathed sword of Jeremiah 47:6 is the same weapon, drawn on the same terms. Ezekiel 21:30 gives the opposite command, 'Return the sword to its sheath,' with the same word for sheath.

'The sword of the LORD devours from one end of the earth to the other. No flesh has peace.' This earlier verse gives the sword a global reach and a settled place in Jeremiah's vocabulary, so the coast of Philistia is only one stop on the road.

The sword that could not rest in Jeremiah 47 is roused again, now against the LORD's own Shepherd. Jesus applies it to Himself in Mark 14:27. The same weapon that threatened the nations is finally turned onto the one who can bear it.

The sword from the mouth of the returning Christ is the final form of the sword in Jeremiah 47. It is no longer an army's weapon but the word of the Rider who judges the nations, and it is not sheathed until the work is done.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with the nations scattered at Babel, and Genesis 10 gives the Philistine line a place in the family of peoples. Their long hostility to Israel starts early: they stand against the patriarchs' wells, against the judges, against Saul and David, and they take the ark itself, 1 Samuel 4. From the start they illustrate a problem the whole Bible keeps meeting. The nations around God's people are not neutral. They are tied to the same fall that marred the garden, and their hostility to the line of promise echoes the war between the serpent and the woman's seed, Genesis 3:15.

Jeremiah 47 is part of the answer to that war. It does not say Philistia will be converted or conquered by Israel. It says the LORD, who owns every sword, will bring an end to a long-standing source of violence. The same oracles section that includes Egypt, Moab, Ammon, Edom and Babylon in chapters 46 to 51 shows that no nation can use its own history or alliances as a shield. Judah is meant to hear that and to stop looking to the coast for rescue.

The story does not end with the sword. Zephaniah 2:6-7 sees the coast as pasture for the remnant of Judah, and Zechariah 9:7 sees a Philistine remnant reckoned among the people of God, 'like a clan in Judah.' Those two small verses point beyond the sentence. In Acts 8 the gospel runs along the Gaza road, and in Acts 2:9-11 many nations hear God's wonders in their own tongues. The sword that could not rest meets its end at the cross, where the Shepherd is struck and the sheep are spared, Zechariah 13:7 and Mark 14:27.

The story closes in a world where the sword is no longer needed. Revelation 19 shows the final judgment with the sword from the Rider's mouth, and then Revelation 21:4 declares that there will be 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain.' The cry of Jeremiah 47:6, 'how long?', is finally answered, not by a sword that sleeps but by a world where nothing remains to be struck. The coastlands that once rang with the clatter of chariots are included in the new creation, where the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24, and every shore belongs to the LORD.

quiz.q: What image opens this oracle to describe the coming invasion, verse 2?

options.text: Waters rising from the north into an overflowing torrent.
options.note: Verse 2 pictures the invasion as a flood sweeping over the land and its people.

options.text: A fire falling from heaven.
options.note: This image belongs to other oracles, not this one.

options.text: A swarm of locusts.
options.note: A common image elsewhere in these oracles, but this chapter specifically pictures rising floodwaters.

options.text: A gentle rain.
options.note: The opposite; the water here is an overwhelming, destructive torrent.

quiz.q: Which Philistine cities are named as silenced by this judgment?

options.text: Gaza and Ashkelon.
options.note: Verse 5 names Gaza's mourning and Ashkelon's silence directly.

options.text: Nineveh and Babylon.
options.note: These are Mesopotamian cities, not Philistine ones, and are judged in other oracles.

options.text: Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
options.note: These are cities of Judah, not the Philistine coast addressed here.

options.text: Tyre and Sidon.
options.note: These Phoenician cities are mentioned as losing their Philistine ally in verse 4, but they are not the cities said to be silenced.

quiz.q: In verse 6, what does the voice plead with the sword of the LORD to do?

options.text: Return to its sheath and be still.
options.note: Verse 6 pictures a desperate wish for the sword to cease and rest.

options.text: Strike harder and faster.
options.note: The opposite of the plea in this verse.

options.text: Turn against Babylon instead.
options.note: Not the content of this plea, which asks simply for the violence to end.

options.text: Reveal who commanded it.
options.note: Verse 7 does reveal this, but the plea itself in verse 6 is simply for the sword to rest.

quiz.q: Why can the sword of the LORD not rest, according to verse 7?

options.text: Because the LORD Himself has commanded and appointed it against Ashkelon and the coastland.
options.note: Verse 7 states this directly as the reason the sword cannot simply stop.

options.text: Because it has a mind of its own, apart from God.
options.note: The text places the sword entirely under the LORD's command, not acting independently.

options.text: Because Egypt refuses to withdraw its army.
options.note: Egypt's campaign sets the historical occasion, but the reason given is the LORD's own command.

options.text: Because the Philistines refuse to surrender.
options.note: Plausible in a general sense, but the text specifically grounds the sword's unrest in the LORD's own appointment.

quiz.q: How does the unstoppable sword of this chapter point forward to Christ?

options.text: It anticipates the certain and unstoppable final judgment Christ will execute at His return.
options.note: Revelation 19:15 pictures Christ's own sword of final judgment, carried out exactly as appointed.

options.text: It shows that Christ has nothing to do with judgment at all.
options.note: Scripture consistently entrusts final judgment to Christ, not apart from Him.

options.text: It suggests judgment is random and unpredictable.
options.note: The opposite is true; this sword moves by direct divine command, not by chance.

options.text: It shows only that ancient warfare was violent.
options.note: True on the surface, but the passage's deeper point is the LORD's sovereign command over the timing of judgment.

questions: The invasion is pictured as a flood no one can hold back. What in your own life feels like rising water you cannot control, and where might God be at work in it?

The prophet, or perhaps the Philistines themselves, plead for the sword to rest, yet it cannot until the LORD's purpose is finished. Where are you asking God to stop something before His work in it is complete?
This chapter reminds Judah's neighbors that no coastline lies outside the LORD's justice. Where do you need reminding that God's rule is not confined to your own concerns?

The sword's certainty and Christ's final judgment are drawn together in Scripture. How does knowing that Christ has already borne judgment's edge for you change how you face the coming day of judgment?

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture tool for Jeremiah 47:1-7.
